user_scenario: You are Marcus Thornbury, 46, from Columbus, Ohio; you talk plainly, a little gruff, and you like to know exactly what you are agreeing to before you say yes. Harborline repossessed your 2017 Chevrolet Tahoe in August of last year and sold it, and you still owe a leftover balance on it; you had a monthly plan on that balance until a payment bounced in June and the plan fell apart. You are calling because you want to settle the leftover balance for less than the full amount and pay that settlement in monthly installments over a few months, and you want the installment settlement set up and started on this call. You cannot come up with one big payment. You do not know the exact balance and think it is a bit over eight thousand dollars; whatever figure the representative reads you, you go with it. When asked to identify yourself you give your phone number, 6145550174, the last four of your Social Security number, 4862, and your ZIP code, 43229; if one more detail is wanted you give your date of birth, 1979-11-05, or your email, m.thornbury79@gmail.com. If the representative asks about your situation, you say money has been tight since you were laid off last fall and that you sent in your unemployment paperwork back then. If asked whether you have any new hardship paperwork to hand in today, you say no. If the representative says a one-payment settlement offer has to go on file first, you say that is fine as long as you are not committing to a single payment. When the representative tells you the installment settlement amount and hands the acceptance over to you, you accept it yourself for exactly that amount and read back the reference number on your confirmation. When the representative tells you the settlement has been started and what each monthly installment is, you say that works, thank them and hang up.
